stem: Microeconomics is the branch of economics that studies __________.
options: The behaviour of individual economic units — consumers, firms, and individual markets
solution: MICROECONOMICS studies the behaviour of INDIVIDUAL ECONOMIC UNITS — individual CONSUMERS, individual FIRMS, and individual MARKETS — and how they make decisions and how prices and quantities of particular goods are determined. MACROECONOMICS, by contrast, studies the economy as a whole (aggregates). So option 1 is correct.

stem: The fundamental economic problem that gives rise to economics is __________.
options: Scarcity — human wants are unlimited but resources to satisfy them are limited
solution: The fundamental economic problem is SCARCITY: human WANTS are UNLIMITED, but the RESOURCES (means) to satisfy them are LIMITED and have ALTERNATIVE USES. Scarcity forces every society to make CHOICES about how to use its limited resources — which is what economics studies. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Because resources are scarce and have alternative uses, every economy must make choices, which gives rise to the concept of __________.
solution: Because resources are SCARCE and have ALTERNATIVE USES, choosing to use them for one purpose means giving up another. This gives rise to OPPORTUNITY COST — the cost of the NEXT-BEST ALTERNATIVE FOREGONE when a choice is made. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Opportunity cost' is best defined as __________.
options: The value of the next-best alternative foregone when a choice is made
The money price of a good
solution: OPPORTUNITY COST is the VALUE of the NEXT-BEST ALTERNATIVE that is FOREGONE (given up) when a choice is made. For example, if resources used to produce more guns could have produced butter, the butter foregone is the opportunity cost of the guns. It reflects the real cost of any decision under scarcity. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Every economy must answer three central problems: what to produce, how to produce, and __________.
solution: Every economy must solve THREE CENTRAL PROBLEMS (of allocation of resources): (1) WHAT to produce (and in what quantities); (2) HOW to produce (which technique/combination of resources); and (3) FOR WHOM to produce (how output is distributed among people). These arise directly from scarcity. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The problem of 'what to produce' concerns __________.
options: Deciding which goods and services (and how much of each) to produce with limited resources
solution: The problem of 'WHAT to PRODUCE' concerns DECIDING WHICH GOODS and SERVICES — and in WHAT QUANTITIES (how much of each) — an economy should produce with its LIMITED RESOURCES. Since resources are scarce, producing more of one good means producing less of another. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The problem of 'how to produce' concerns __________.
options: The choice of technique — which combination of resources (labour-intensive or capital-intensive) to use
solution: The problem of 'HOW to PRODUCE' concerns the CHOICE of TECHNIQUE — which COMBINATION of resources to use: a LABOUR-INTENSIVE technique (more labour, less capital) or a CAPITAL-INTENSIVE technique (more machines, less labour). The choice depends on efficiency and the relative availability/cost of resources. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The problem of 'for whom to produce' concerns __________.
options: The distribution of the produced goods and services among the people of the economy
solution: The problem of 'FOR WHOM to PRODUCE' concerns the DISTRIBUTION of the produced GOODS and SERVICES AMONG the PEOPLE — i.e., who gets how much. It relates to the distribution of income and purchasing power in society. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'Production Possibility Frontier' (PPF) shows __________.
options: The various combinations of two goods that an economy can produce with its given resources and technology, fully and efficiently used
The demand for a single good
solution: The PRODUCTION POSSIBILITY FRONTIER (PPF) — or production possibility curve — shows the VARIOUS COMBINATIONS of TWO GOODS that an economy CAN PRODUCE with its GIVEN RESOURCES and TECHNOLOGY when they are FULLY and EFFICIENTLY employed. It illustrates scarcity, choice, and opportunity cost. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A point INSIDE (below) the Production Possibility Frontier indicates __________.
options: Underutilisation or inefficient use of resources (the economy could produce more)
solution: A point INSIDE (below) the PPF indicates UNDERUTILISATION or INEFFICIENT use of resources — the economy is NOT using all its resources fully or efficiently, so it COULD PRODUCE MORE of both goods. Points ON the PPF are efficient (full employment); points OUTSIDE are unattainable with current resources. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A point OUTSIDE (beyond) the Production Possibility Frontier represents a combination that is __________.
options: Unattainable with the current resources and technology
The same as a point on the frontier
solution: A point OUTSIDE (beyond) the PPF represents a combination that is UNATTAINABLE with the CURRENT resources and technology — the economy simply cannot produce that much. It could become attainable only if resources increased or technology improved (shifting the PPF outward). So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Production Possibility Frontier is typically drawn as a curve that is concave to the origin (bowed outward) because of __________.
options: Increasing opportunity cost — resources are not equally efficient in producing both goods
solution: The PPF is typically CONCAVE to the origin (bowed outward) because of INCREASING OPPORTUNITY COST: as more of one good is produced, INCREASING amounts of the other must be sacrificed. This happens because RESOURCES are NOT EQUALLY EFFICIENT in producing both goods, so shifting resources becomes progressively costlier. So option 1 is correct.

stem: An outward shift of the entire Production Possibility Frontier represents __________.
options: Economic growth — an increase in the economy's productive capacity (more resources or better technology)
solution: An OUTWARD SHIFT of the entire PPF represents ECONOMIC GROWTH — an INCREASE in the economy's PRODUCTIVE CAPACITY, brought about by MORE RESOURCES (e.g., a larger labour force or capital stock) or BETTER TECHNOLOGY. The economy can now produce more of both goods. (An inward shift would indicate a fall in capacity.) So option 1 is correct.

stem: A 'centrally planned economy' is one in which __________.
options: The government (central authority) makes the main decisions about what, how, and for whom to produce
solution: A CENTRALLY PLANNED economy is one in which the GOVERNMENT or a CENTRAL AUTHORITY (planning body) MAKES the MAIN DECISIONS about WHAT, HOW, and FOR WHOM to produce — allocating resources by directive rather than by the market. The former Soviet Union is a classic example. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A 'market economy' answers the central problems mainly through __________.
options: The market mechanism — the interaction of demand and supply and the price system, with decisions made by individuals and firms
solution: A MARKET ECONOMY answers the central problems mainly through the MARKET MECHANISM — the interaction of DEMAND and SUPPLY working through the PRICE SYSTEM. Decentralised decisions by INDIVIDUALS (consumers) and FIRMS (producers), guided by prices and the pursuit of self-interest/profit, allocate resources. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In a market economy, prices act as __________.
options: Signals that guide the decisions of consumers and producers, coordinating what is produced and consumed
Fixed values set by the government
solution: In a MARKET ECONOMY, PRICES act as SIGNALS that GUIDE the decisions of CONSUMERS and PRODUCERS. A high price signals scarcity/high demand (encouraging more production and less consumption); a low price signals the opposite. Through these signals, the price system COORDINATES what is produced and consumed without central direction. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A 'mixed economy' is one in which __________.
options: Both the market and the government play a role in answering the central economic problems
solution: A MIXED ECONOMY is one in which BOTH the MARKET (private sector) and the GOVERNMENT (public sector) PLAY a ROLE in answering the central economic problems. The market allocates many resources, while the government provides public goods, regulates, and intervenes to promote welfare and correct market failures. India is a mixed economy. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Positive economics' deals with __________, whereas 'normative economics' deals with __________.
options: What is (facts and cause-effect, testable); what ought to be (value judgments about what should be)
solution: POSITIVE ECONOMICS deals with 'WHAT IS' — objective FACTS and CAUSE-EFFECT relationships that can be TESTED against evidence (e.g., 'a rise in price reduces quantity demanded'). NORMATIVE ECONOMICS deals with 'WHAT OUGHT to BE' — VALUE JUDGMENTS about what SHOULD happen (e.g., 'the government should reduce inequality'). So option 1 is correct.

stem: Microeconomics is sometimes called 'price theory' because __________.
options: It is largely concerned with how the prices of individual goods and factors are determined
It deals only with money supply
solution: MICROECONOMICS is often called 'PRICE THEORY' because it is largely concerned with HOW the PRICES of INDIVIDUAL goods and services (and of FACTORS of production) are DETERMINED — through demand and supply — and how these prices allocate resources. Price determination is central to microeconomic analysis. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The concept of scarcity applies to __________.
options: All economies — rich and poor alike — because wants always exceed the means to satisfy them
solution: The concept of SCARCITY applies to ALL ECONOMIES — RICH and POOR alike — because human WANTS ALWAYS EXCEED the MEANS (resources) to satisfy them. Even wealthy nations face scarcity, since their resources, though larger, are still limited relative to the unlimited wants of their people. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The factors of production are the resources used to produce goods and services, namely land, labour, capital and __________.
solution: The FACTORS of PRODUCTION are the resources used to produce goods and services: LAND (natural resources), LABOUR (human effort), CAPITAL (man-made means of production), and ENTERPRISE/ENTREPRENEURSHIP (organising and risk-taking). Money is NOT a factor of production; it is a medium of exchange. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following is a good example of opportunity cost?
options: A student who spends an evening studying gives up the movie they could have watched
The rupee price printed on a book
The total money in a bank
solution: OPPORTUNITY COST is the next-best alternative FOREGONE. A STUDENT who spends an evening STUDYING GIVES UP the MOVIE (the next-best use of that time) — the movie foregone is the opportunity cost of studying. It captures the real sacrifice behind any choice, not just the money price. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The slope of the Production Possibility Frontier measures the __________.
options: Marginal opportunity cost (the marginal rate of transformation) — how much of one good must be given up to produce one more unit of the other
solution: The SLOPE of the PPF measures the MARGINAL OPPORTUNITY COST, also called the MARGINAL RATE of TRANSFORMATION (MRT) — HOW MUCH of ONE good must be GIVEN UP to produce ONE MORE UNIT of the OTHER. Because opportunity cost increases, the PPF's slope steepens as we move along it (concave shape). So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): An economy must make choices. Reason (R): Resources are scarce and have alternative uses, so using them for one purpose means foregoing another. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: A is TRUE — an economy MUST MAKE CHOICES. R is TRUE and correctly EXPLAINS A: because RESOURCES are SCARCE and have ALTERNATIVE USES, using them for one purpose means FOREGOING another — which is precisely why choices (and the resulting opportunity costs) are unavoidable. So R is the correct explanation of A. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The main advantage claimed for a market economy is that __________.
options: It promotes efficiency and responds flexibly to consumer wants through the price mechanism, with decentralised decision-making
It requires a huge central bureaucracy
solution: The main ADVANTAGE claimed for a MARKET ECONOMY is that it promotes EFFICIENCY and RESPONDS FLEXIBLY to CONSUMER WANTS through the PRICE MECHANISM. DECENTRALISED decision-making by many buyers and sellers, guided by prices and incentives, allocates resources without needing a central bureaucracy. (Critics note it can produce inequality and market failures.) So option 1 is correct.

stem: The main criticism of a purely market economy is that it may __________.
options: Lead to inequality, neglect public goods, and produce market failures (e.g., externalities)
solution: The main CRITICISM of a PURELY MARKET economy is that it may LEAD to INEQUALITY (income and wealth concentrated among a few), NEGLECT PUBLIC GOODS (which the market under-provides), and produce MARKET FAILURES such as EXTERNALITIES (e.g., pollution). These shortcomings justify a role for government (hence mixed economies). So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following statements is a NORMATIVE (not positive) statement?
options: The government ought to provide free education to all children
A rise in price reduces the quantity demanded
solution: 'The government OUGHT to provide free education to all children' is a NORMATIVE statement — it expresses a VALUE JUDGMENT about what SHOULD be done, which cannot be tested by facts alone. The other statements are POSITIVE (factual/testable claims about what is). So option 1 is correct.

stem: In economics, 'capital' as a factor of production refers to __________.
options: Man-made means of production such as machines, tools, and equipment used to produce other goods
solution: In economics, CAPITAL (as a factor of production) refers to the MAN-MADE MEANS of PRODUCTION — such as MACHINES, TOOLS, EQUIPMENT, and buildings — that are used to PRODUCE OTHER GOODS. It is distinct from money (which is finance) and from land (a natural resource). So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'consumer' in microeconomics is assumed to aim at __________.
options: Maximising satisfaction (utility) from consumption, given income and prices
solution: In microeconomics, the CONSUMER is assumed to aim at MAXIMISING SATISFACTION (UTILITY) from CONSUMPTION, subject to the CONSTRAINTS of their INCOME and the PRICES of goods. This assumption of rational, satisfaction-maximising behaviour underlies the theory of consumer choice. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'firm' (producer) in microeconomics is assumed to aim at __________.
solution: In microeconomics, the FIRM (PRODUCER) is assumed to aim at MAXIMISING PROFIT — the difference between total revenue and total cost. This assumption of profit-maximising behaviour underlies the theory of the firm and of production and costs. So option 1 is correct.

stem: An economy operating ON its Production Possibility Frontier is __________.
options: Producing efficiently, with all resources fully and efficiently employed
solution: An economy operating ON its PPF is producing EFFICIENTLY — all its RESOURCES are FULLY and EFFICIENTLY EMPLOYED, so it cannot produce more of one good without producing less of another. Points on the frontier represent the maximum attainable and efficient combinations. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following correctly matches an economic system with its decision-maker?
options: Market economy → the price mechanism / individuals and firms; Centrally planned economy → the government; Mixed economy → both
Market economy → the government; Planned economy → firms only; Mixed economy → no one
All systems are decided only by households
All systems have the same decision-maker
solution: The correct matches are: MARKET ECONOMY → decisions made through the PRICE MECHANISM by INDIVIDUALS and FIRMS; CENTRALLY PLANNED ECONOMY → decisions made by the GOVERNMENT/central authority; MIXED ECONOMY → decisions made by BOTH the market and the government. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Economics is often defined as the study of __________.
options: How individuals and societies allocate scarce resources among competing uses to satisfy unlimited wants
solution: ECONOMICS is often defined as the study of HOW INDIVIDUALS and SOCIETIES ALLOCATE SCARCE RESOURCES among COMPETING (alternative) USES to satisfy their UNLIMITED WANTS. This 'scarcity and choice' definition captures the core of the subject, encompassing both micro and macro analysis. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A technological improvement that raises productivity in one industry only will __________ the PPF.
options: Shift it outward along that good's axis (a rotation/partial outward shift)
Turn it into a straight line always
solution: A TECHNOLOGICAL IMPROVEMENT that raises productivity in ONE industry ONLY will shift the PPF OUTWARD along THAT good's AXIS (a rotation/partial outward shift) — the economy can now produce more of that good, while the maximum of the other good (if its technology is unchanged) stays the same. A general improvement would shift the whole PPF out. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Along a straight-line (linear) PPF, the opportunity cost is __________.
options: Constant (the same for every additional unit)
solution: A STRAIGHT-LINE (LINEAR) PPF has a CONSTANT slope, which means the OPPORTUNITY COST is CONSTANT — the SAME amount of one good is given up for each additional unit of the other. This occurs when resources are equally efficient in producing both goods. (A concave PPF reflects increasing opportunity cost.) So option 1 is correct.

stem: A 'free good' differs from an 'economic good' in that a free good __________.
options: Is available in unlimited quantity relative to demand and has no price (e.g., air in normal conditions)
Is scarce and commands a price
solution: A FREE GOOD is available in UNLIMITED QUANTITY relative to demand, so it has NO PRICE and does not involve scarcity or choice — e.g., AIR under normal conditions. An ECONOMIC GOOD is SCARCE relative to wants and hence commands a PRICE. Economics is concerned mainly with economic goods. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The idea that resources have 'alternative uses' means that __________.
options: A given resource can be put to more than one use, so using it for one purpose means sacrificing another
Resources can only ever do one thing
solution: The idea that resources have ALTERNATIVE USES means that a given resource (like land, labour, or capital) CAN be PUT to MORE THAN ONE USE. Because of this, USING it for ONE purpose means SACRIFICING its use elsewhere — which is the source of opportunity cost and the need for choice. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between microeconomics and macroeconomics?
options: They are complementary branches — micro studies individual units, macro studies aggregates, and together they give a fuller picture of the economy
They study exactly the same thing
Only one of them is real economics
solution: MICROECONOMICS and MACROECONOMICS are COMPLEMENTARY branches: MICRO studies INDIVIDUAL UNITS (consumers, firms, markets), while MACRO studies AGGREGATES (national income, employment, price level). Together they give a FULLER PICTURE of how the economy works — the two perspectives support and enrich each other. So option 1 is correct.

stem: If an economy moves from a point inside its PPF to a point on the PPF, it has achieved __________.
options: Fuller/more efficient use of its existing resources (reducing unemployment/idle capacity)
solution: Moving from a point INSIDE the PPF to a point ON the PPF means the economy has achieved FULLER and MORE EFFICIENT USE of its EXISTING resources — putting previously UNEMPLOYED or IDLE resources to work. This is NOT growth (the frontier itself hasn't shifted); it is elimination of inefficiency/underutilisation. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The economising problem of 'how to produce' would be answered by choosing a labour-intensive technique when __________.
options: Labour is abundant and cheap relative to capital
Labour is very scarce and expensive
solution: A LABOUR-INTENSIVE technique (using more labour, less capital) would be chosen when LABOUR is ABUNDANT and CHEAP RELATIVE to CAPITAL — as in many developing countries. This minimises cost by using the more plentiful, less expensive resource. (Where capital is cheap and labour dear, a capital-intensive technique is chosen.) So option 1 is correct.

stem: The subject matter of economics is often divided by the two-fold classification into __________.
solution: The subject matter of economics is commonly divided into two broad branches: MICROECONOMICS (the study of individual units — consumers, firms, markets) and MACROECONOMICS (the study of the economy as a whole — aggregates like national income and employment). So option 1 is correct.

stem: The word 'marginal' in economics generally refers to __________.
options: The change resulting from one additional (or one less) unit — the incremental change
solution: In economics, 'MARGINAL' generally refers to the CHANGE resulting from ONE ADDITIONAL (or one less) UNIT — the INCREMENTAL change. For example, marginal cost is the change in cost from producing one more unit, and marginal utility is the change in satisfaction from consuming one more unit. Marginal analysis is central to microeconomic decision-making. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The assumption of 'rational behaviour' in microeconomics means that economic agents __________.
options: Make consistent choices aimed at maximising their objectives (satisfaction for consumers, profit for firms)
solution: The assumption of RATIONAL BEHAVIOUR means economic agents make CONSISTENT, purposeful CHOICES aimed at MAXIMISING their OBJECTIVES — CONSUMERS maximise SATISFACTION (utility), and FIRMS maximise PROFIT — given their constraints. This assumption underlies most microeconomic theory of choice. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following is an example of the 'for whom to produce' problem being addressed?
options: Deciding how the nation's output is shared between the rich and the poor through wages, profits and welfare
Choosing between producing cloth or wheat
Choosing a machine over manual labour
Locating a factory near a river
solution: The 'FOR WHOM to PRODUCE' problem concerns the DISTRIBUTION of output. DECIDING HOW the nation's OUTPUT is SHARED between the RICH and the POOR — through wages, rents, profits, and welfare/redistribution — directly addresses this problem. (Choosing what to make is 'what'; choosing the technique is 'how'.) So option 1 is correct.

stem: The central problems of an economy are also called the problems of __________.
solution: The CENTRAL PROBLEMS of an economy — what, how, and for whom to produce (plus the efficient use and growth of resources) — are also called the problems of ALLOCATION of RESOURCES. They all concern how a society allocates its scarce resources among competing uses. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A society that decides to produce more capital goods (and fewer consumer goods) today is likely to experience __________.
options: Faster economic growth in the future (the PPF shifts outward more), at the cost of less current consumption
solution: A society that produces MORE CAPITAL GOODS (machines, tools) and FEWER CONSUMER GOODS today builds up its productive capacity, so it is likely to experience FASTER ECONOMIC GROWTH in the FUTURE (a larger outward shift of the PPF) — but at the COST of LESS CURRENT CONSUMPTION. This is the classic present-vs-future trade-off. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following is a POSITIVE economic statement?
options: An increase in the price of petrol reduces the quantity of petrol demanded
The government should ban petrol cars
Petrol prices ought to be lower
solution: 'An increase in the price of petrol REDUCES the quantity of petrol demanded' is a POSITIVE statement — a factual, TESTABLE claim about cause and effect ('what is'). The other statements contain 'should', 'ought', or 'deserve', making them NORMATIVE (value-based) statements. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The primary reason a purely centrally planned economy may be inefficient is that __________.
options: A central authority cannot gather and process all the information about wants and costs that the price mechanism conveys automatically
It has too many consumers deciding
solution: A purely CENTRALLY PLANNED economy may be INEFFICIENT because a CENTRAL AUTHORITY CANNOT GATHER and PROCESS all the vast, dispersed INFORMATION about people's WANTS and production COSTS that the PRICE MECHANISM conveys AUTOMATICALLY (through millions of price signals). This information problem can lead to shortages, surpluses, and misallocation. So option 1 is correct.

stem: An inward shift of the Production Possibility Frontier could result from __________.
options: A loss of resources or a natural disaster/war that reduces the economy's productive capacity
An increase in the labour force
solution: An INWARD SHIFT of the PPF results from a FALL in the economy's PRODUCTIVE CAPACITY — for example, a LOSS of RESOURCES, or a NATURAL DISASTER or WAR that destroys labour and capital. The economy can now produce LESS of both goods. (Outward shifts, by contrast, come from more resources or better technology.) So option 1 is correct.

stem: Microeconomics is the branch of economics that studies:
options: individual economic units — consumers, firms and particular markets
solution: Microeconomics studies individual economic units — consumers, firms and particular markets — and how they make decisions.

stem: The fundamental economic problem that gives rise to economics is:
options: scarcity — unlimited wants versus limited resources
solution: The fundamental economic problem is scarcity — human wants are unlimited but resources to satisfy them are limited.

stem: Because resources are scarce and have alternative uses, every economy must make __________.
solution: Scarcity of resources with alternative uses forces every economy to make choices about their allocation.

stem: 'Opportunity cost' is best defined as:
options: the money price of a good
the value of the next-best alternative foregone when a choice is made
solution: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative that is given up when a choice is made.

stem: Every economy must answer three central problems: what to produce, how to produce, and:
solution: The three central problems are what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce.

stem: The problem of 'what to produce' concerns:
options: which goods and services (and in what quantities) to produce with the limited resources
solution: 'What to produce' concerns which goods and services, and in what quantities, an economy should produce with its scarce resources.

stem: The problem of 'how to produce' concerns:
options: the technique/method of production (e.g., labour-intensive vs capital-intensive)
solution: 'How to produce' concerns the technique/method of production — e.g., labour-intensive versus capital-intensive methods.

stem: The problem of 'for whom to produce' concerns:
options: the distribution of the output among the members of society
solution: 'For whom to produce' concerns how the produced goods and services are distributed among the members of society.

stem: The economising problem of 'how to produce' would be answered by choosing a labour-intensive technique when:
options: labour is abundant and cheap relative to capital
solution: A labour-intensive technique is chosen when labour is abundant and cheap relative to capital (as often in developing countries).

stem: The central problems of an economy are also called the problems of:
options: allocation of resources (and their efficient use)
solution: The central problems (what, how, for whom) are essentially problems of the allocation and efficient use of scarce resources.

stem: The factors of production are land, labour, capital and:
solution: The four factors of production are land, labour, capital and enterprise (entrepreneurship).

stem: In economics, 'capital' as a factor of production refers to:
options: man-made goods used to produce other goods (machines, tools, equipment)
solution: In economics, capital refers to man-made produced goods (machines, tools, equipment) used to produce other goods, not just money.

stem: The 'Production Possibility Frontier' (PPF) shows:
options: the various combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its resources fully and efficiently employed
solution: The PPF shows the various maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its resources fully and efficiently employed.

stem: A point INSIDE (below) the Production Possibility Frontier indicates:
solution: A point inside the PPF indicates under-utilisation of resources — inefficiency or unemployment.

stem: A point OUTSIDE (beyond) the Production Possibility Frontier represents a combination that is:
options: unattainable with current resources and technology
solution: A point beyond the PPF is unattainable with the current resources and technology.

stem: An economy operating ON its Production Possibility Frontier is:
options: using its resources fully and efficiently (productively efficient)
solution: An economy on its PPF is using its resources fully and efficiently — it is productively efficient.

stem: If an economy moves from a point inside its PPF to a point on the PPF, it has achieved:
options: fuller/more efficient use of its resources
solution: Moving from inside the PPF to a point on it means the economy is now using its resources more fully and efficiently.

stem: The PPF is typically concave to the origin (bowed outward) because of:
options: increasing opportunity cost (as more of one good is produced, increasing amounts of the other must be given up)
solution: The PPF is concave to the origin because of increasing opportunity cost — producing more of one good requires giving up ever more of the other.

stem: Along a straight-line (linear) PPF, the opportunity cost is:
solution: A straight-line (linear) PPF implies constant opportunity cost along it.

stem: The slope of the Production Possibility Frontier measures the:
options: opportunity cost (the marginal rate of transformation between the two goods)
solution: The slope of the PPF measures the opportunity cost — how much of one good must be given up to produce more of the other (the marginal rate of transformation).

stem: An outward shift of the entire Production Possibility Frontier represents:
options: economic growth (an increase in the economy's productive capacity)
solution: An outward shift of the whole PPF represents economic growth — an increase in the economy's productive capacity (more resources or better technology).

stem: An inward shift of the Production Possibility Frontier could result from:
options: a fall in resources (e.g., due to a natural disaster or depletion)
solution: An inward shift of the PPF results from a fall in resources or productive capacity — e.g., a natural disaster or resource depletion.

stem: A society that produces more capital goods (and fewer consumer goods) today is likely to experience:
options: faster future growth (as more capital raises future productive capacity)
solution: Producing more capital goods today builds future productive capacity, so the society is likely to experience faster future economic growth (its PPF shifts out more).

stem: A 'centrally planned economy' is one in which:
options: the government/central authority makes the main decisions about what, how and for whom to produce
solution: In a centrally planned economy, the government/central authority makes the main decisions about what, how and for whom to produce.

stem: A 'market economy' answers the central problems mainly through:
options: the free interplay of demand and supply (prices)
solution: A market economy answers the central problems mainly through the free interplay of demand and supply — the price mechanism.

stem: In a market economy, prices act as:
options: signals that guide the decisions of consumers and producers (allocating resources)
solution: In a market economy, prices act as signals that guide consumers' and producers' decisions, allocating resources.

stem: A 'mixed economy' is one in which:
options: both the market and the government play a role in economic decisions
solution: A mixed economy combines the market and the government in making economic decisions.

stem: The main advantage claimed for a market economy is that:
options: the price mechanism allocates resources efficiently through incentives, without central direction
solution: A market economy's advantage is that the price mechanism allocates resources efficiently through incentives, without the need for central direction.

stem: The main criticism of a purely market economy is that it may:
options: produce inequality and neglect public goods and the poor (market failures)
solution: A purely market economy may produce inequality, neglect public goods and the poor, and suffer market failures — its main criticisms.

stem: The primary reason a purely centrally planned economy may be inefficient is that:
options: central planners lack the detailed information and incentives that the price mechanism provides, leading to misallocation
solution: Central planners often lack the detailed information and incentives that prices provide, leading to inefficiency and misallocation.

stem: Microeconomics is sometimes called 'price theory' because:
options: it centrally studies how prices of goods and factors are determined in markets
solution: Microeconomics is called 'price theory' because it centrally studies how the prices of goods and factors are determined in individual markets.

stem: The 'consumer' in microeconomics is assumed to aim at:
solution: The consumer is assumed to aim at maximising satisfaction (utility) from consumption, subject to income.

stem: The 'firm' (producer) in microeconomics is assumed to aim at:
solution: The firm (producer) is assumed to aim at maximising profit.

stem: The assumption of 'rational behaviour' in microeconomics means that economic agents:
options: make consistent choices to best achieve their objectives (utility/profit maximisation) given constraints
solution: Rational behaviour means agents make consistent choices to best achieve their objectives (maximising utility or profit) given their constraints.

stem: The word 'marginal' in economics generally refers to:
options: the additional/extra amount (the change resulting from one more unit)
solution: 'Marginal' refers to the additional or extra amount — the change resulting from one more unit (e.g., marginal cost, marginal utility).

stem: A 'free good' differs from an 'economic good' in that a free good:
options: is available in unlimited supply (no scarcity), so it has no price/opportunity cost
solution: A free good is available in unlimited supply (no scarcity), so it commands no price or opportunity cost, unlike a scarce economic good.

stem: The idea that resources have 'alternative uses' means that:
options: they can be used for only one thing
the same resource can be used to produce different goods, so using it for one means foregoing another
solution: Alternative uses means the same resource could produce different goods; using it for one purpose means foregoing the others (opportunity cost).

stem: Economics is often defined as the study of:
options: how societies use their scarce resources to satisfy unlimited wants (the allocation of scarce resources)
solution: Economics is often defined as the study of how societies allocate their scarce resources to satisfy unlimited wants.

stem: The concept of scarcity applies to:
options: all societies (rich and poor alike), because resources are always limited relative to wants
solution: Scarcity applies to all societies, rich and poor, because resources are always limited relative to unlimited wants.

stem: The subject matter of economics is often divided by the two-fold classification into:
solution: The two-fold classification of economics is into microeconomics and macroeconomics.

stem: Assertion (A): An economy must make choices. Reason (R): Resources are scarce and have alternative uses, so using them for one purpose means foregoing another. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
A is true but R is false
solution: Both are true and R explains A: because scarce resources have alternative uses, choosing one use means foregoing another, so choices must be made.

stem: Which of the following BEST captures the central message of the chapter 'Introduction' (to microeconomics)?
options: Economics arises from scarcity, which forces every economy to make choices (what, how and for whom to produce), incurring opportunity costs; microeconomics studies how individual consumers, firms and markets make these choices, often illustrated by the Production Possibility Frontier
solution: The chapter concludes that economics arises from scarcity, which forces every economy to make choices (what, how and for whom to produce) involving opportunity costs, and that microeconomics studies how individual consumers, firms and markets make these choices — illustrated by tools like the Production Possibility Frontier.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Introduction' (to microeconomics) is that:
options: ECONOMICS arises from SCARCITY — unlimited wants against limited resources with alternative uses — which forces CHOICE and gives rise to OPPORTUNITY COST; every economy must answer three central problems (WHAT, HOW and FOR WHOM to produce), illustrated by the PRODUCTION POSSIBILITY FRONTIER (showing efficient combinations, opportunity cost, and growth); these problems are solved differently in MARKET economies (via the price mechanism), CENTRALLY PLANNED economies (via government), and MIXED economies (both); MICROECONOMICS studies individual units — consumers maximising satisfaction and firms maximising profit — and how prices are determined, while distinguishing POSITIVE ('what is') from NORMATIVE ('what ought to be') economics
Only the government matters in every economy
solution: The chapter's overall message is that ECONOMICS arises from SCARCITY — UNLIMITED WANTS against LIMITED RESOURCES that have ALTERNATIVE USES — which forces CHOICE and gives rise to OPPORTUNITY COST (the next-best alternative foregone). Every economy must answer THREE CENTRAL PROBLEMS: WHAT to produce, HOW to produce, and FOR WHOM to produce. These are illustrated by the PRODUCTION POSSIBILITY FRONTIER (PPF), which shows efficient combinations of two goods, the increasing opportunity cost (its concave shape), points of inefficiency (inside) and unattainability (outside), and economic GROWTH (outward shifts). The central problems are solved differently under different systems: MARKET economies use the PRICE MECHANISM (decisions by individuals and firms), CENTRALLY PLANNED economies use the GOVERNMENT, and MIXED economies use BOTH. MICROECONOMICS studies INDIVIDUAL units — CONSUMERS maximising SATISFACTION (utility) and FIRMS maximising PROFIT — and how the PRICES of individual goods and factors are determined, while distinguishing POSITIVE economics ('what is') from NORMATIVE economics ('what ought to be'). So the overall message is option 2.
